The empirical age-to-age factors for paid loss decay smoothly and monotonically from 2.55 at 11-23 months down through the 100+ month range, essentially flattening to 1.0000 by 227-239 months and then holding in a tight 1.002-1.008 band through 275-287 months (CVs at the tail under 0.02, no meaningful slope reversals in the smoothed averages). This is a textbook slow, well-behaved convergence pattern that an inverse power curve (Bondy) is built to extrapolate: it produces a modest, controlled tail factor of 1.006 that is consistent with the last several observed LDFs continuing to inch toward unity rather than either flattening instantly or blowing up. Diagnostics support this choice: materiality_ok is True, the tail represents under 0.1% of the total CDF (pct_of_cdf=0.093), and leave-one-out cross-validation shows a very stable fit (loo_std_dev=0.0016, loo_min/max tightly bounded 1.0046-1.0083), with sensitivity to +/-10% and +/-20% assumption shocks producing correspondingly modest, well-behaved reserve deltas. Compared to alternatives: the exponential-decay methods (exp_dev_quick and especially exp_dev_quick_exact_last) fit an exponential to what is actually a nearly flat, noisy tail and produce implausibly large tail factors (1.17 and 1.52 respectively) that are not supported by the data - the triangle simply does not show that much remaining development, and both fail materiality_ok. Skurnick is even more extreme (tail=2.93, r_squared only 0.46, pct_of_cdf=9.3%, fails materiality) and is not credible here. McClenahan produces an essentially negligible tail factor (1.00002) that is arguably too aggressive given the empirical data still shows non-zero LDFs (1.004-1.008) through 275-287 months - it understates the residual development implied by the observed pattern. The modified Bondy variants give a similar tail factor (~1.012) to standard Bondy but fail the materiality check, making standard Bondy the cleanest, best-supported selection.
